questions.prompt: A reaction is independently known to be thermodynamically favored under the stored conditions, yet no measurable conversion occurs over a week. Which explanation is consistent?
options: Its free-energy change must actually be zero solely because no change is seen
A high activation barrier makes the reaction kinetically slow.
All thermodynamically favored reactions finish immediately
The reactants must have no thermal motion
questions.explanation: B is correct. Thermodynamic driving force and the rate of crossing a barrier are separate properties. A is incorrect: lack of measurable conversion does not establish equilibrium. C is incorrect: favorability does not imply rapid kinetics. D is incorrect: a small reactive fraction can make conversion slow despite ongoing motion.

questions.prompt: A catalyst greatly accelerates a slow favorable reaction at constant temperature. What does it primarily change?
options: The sign of ΔG° from positive to negative
Only the product molar mass
The final equilibrium constant by the same factor as the rate
The reaction pathway and activation barrier, not the equilibrium free-energy difference.
questions.explanation: D is correct. A catalyst allows faster approach through a different route while preserving reactant/product thermodynamics. A is incorrect: catalysis does not redefine the standard free-energy difference. B is incorrect: catalysts do not change the chemical identities in the specified net reaction. C is incorrect: equilibrium constants are not multiplied by catalytic acceleration.

questions.prompt: Two pathways lead from the same reactants to the same products at the same conditions. PathI has activation energy80 kJ/mol and pathII has40 kJ/mol. What can be concluded about the reaction free-energy change?
options: It is the same for both pathways, even though their rates can differ.
It is twice as large for pathI
It must be negative only for pathII
It is zero for both because two paths exist
questions.explanation: A is correct. Initial and final states determine the thermodynamic difference; barriers describe the routes. B is incorrect: activation-energy magnitude is not the reaction free-energy difference. C is incorrect: lowering a barrier does not change reaction favorability. D is incorrect: the existence of alternate paths does not require equilibrium.

questions.prompt: A fuel-oxidizer mixture is thermodynamically favored to react under its initial conditions but requires an ignition event to react rapidly. Why?
options: Ignition permanently changes the equilibrium constant into a rate constant
A favorable reaction cannot require any initiation
Ignition supplies an initial population capable of crossing the activation barrier.
Ignition must create atoms missing from the balanced reaction
questions.explanation: C is correct. Starting a thermodynamically favorable reaction can still require overcoming a kinetic barrier. A is incorrect: those quantities remain distinct. B is incorrect: that confuses thermodynamics with kinetics. D is incorrect: the trigger need not add net reaction atoms.

questions.prompt: A reaction with positive ΔG° is studied under standard conditions. Can an ordinary catalyst alone make its forward standard free-energy change negative?
options: Yes, any sufficiently powerful catalyst reverses ΔG°
Yes, but only if it is a solid catalyst
Yes, because only the forward reaction is catalyzed
No; the catalyst cannot change that thermodynamic difference.
questions.explanation: D is correct. External energy, coupling or changed conditions may alter the situation, but catalysis alone only modifies pathways. A is incorrect: barrier reduction does not change the endpoint free-energy difference. B is incorrect: catalyst phase does not override thermodynamics. C is incorrect: a catalytic pathway also supports the reverse process.

questions.prompt: A gas reaction becomes much faster on heating. What does that observation alone establish?
options: The reaction necessarily changed from unfavorable to favorable
Its kinetics changed; the sign of its thermodynamic driving force is not determined by speed alone.
Its equilibrium constant must be numerically equal to the new rate
The activation barrier must have vanished entirely
questions.explanation: B is correct. Higher temperature can increase the reactive collision population without the rate measurement itself identifying equilibrium favorability. A is incorrect: a rate increase does not prove a sign change. C is incorrect: kinetic and equilibrium quantities differ. D is incorrect: more particles can cross a finite barrier.

questions.prompt: Why can a gas mixture have many collisions but extremely slow chemical conversion?
options: Every collision must form product, so slow reaction is impossible
A negative ΔG requires zero activation energy
Only a small fraction of collisions may have sufficient energy and suitable orientation.
Slow conversion proves particles are motionless
questions.explanation: C is correct. Total collision frequency is not the same as successful reactive collision frequency. A is incorrect: most collisions can be unproductive. B is incorrect: free-energy difference does not set the barrier to zero. D is incorrect: collisions demonstrate motion.

questions.prompt: A sample remains chemically unchanged for months. What additional evidence is needed before interpreting it as equilibrium rather than kinetic persistence?
options: Evidence that opposing processes are balanced under the actual conditions.
Only a larger sample of the same unchanged material
Proof that its standard enthalpy is negative
A claim that all stable-looking samples must have ΔG°=0
questions.explanation: A is correct. Macroscopic constancy alone does not distinguish dynamic equilibrium from a reaction too slow to observe. B is incorrect: more material does not by itself identify balanced rates. C is incorrect: enthalpy sign alone does not establish equilibrium. D is incorrect: appearance is not a thermodynamic measurement.

questions.prompt: A solid conversion is assigned a negative free-energy change under the stated conditions but has a very high rearrangement barrier. Which description is appropriate?
options: Thermodynamically unfavorable solely because it is slow
At equilibrium solely because the solid is visible
Thermodynamically favored but kinetically hindered.
Certain to complete instantly because ΔG is negative
questions.explanation: C is correct. The driving force favors products, while slow atomic rearrangement limits the observed rate. A is incorrect: slowness concerns the barrier, not the given driving force. B is incorrect: persistence does not prove equal opposing rates. D is incorrect: favorability alone does not specify a time scale.

questions.prompt: A slow favorable reaction is accelerated by a catalyst. At equilibrium, both catalyzed forward and reverse rates are greater than before catalyst addition. Why is there still no net change?
options: The reverse reaction must stop at equilibrium
The catalyst consumes exactly all product formed
The equilibrium constant must decrease until both rates become zero
The two opposing rates remain equal.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Catalysis can increase both balanced rates without changing the equilibrium composition. A is incorrect: dynamic equilibrium includes reverse events. B is incorrect: the catalyst is not a net sink for the reaction product. C is incorrect: rates need not vanish and K is unchanged at fixed temperature.

questions.prompt: An energy diagram has products lower than reactants, but a tall intermediate barrier. Which design change could increase rate while retaining the same net reactants and products at the same temperature?
options: Raise the product energy solely to make ΔG more negative
Provide a catalytic path with a lower barrier.
Remove all collisions between reactants
Assume the existing tall barrier is irrelevant because products are lower
questions.explanation: B is correct. Changing the pathway can reduce kinetic hindrance without moving the endpoint energy levels. A is incorrect: raising product energy does not make the forward thermodynamic change more favorable. C is incorrect: that prevents rather than accelerates conversion. D is incorrect: the barrier still controls the reactive population.
